content.title: ESPN's Fab Five documentary chronicles iconic Michigan basketball era
content.text: AP File PhotoThe Fab Five, from left: Jimmy King, Juwan Howard, Chris Webber, Jalen Rose and Ray Jackson.I was 13 years old when the Fab Five first arrived at the University of Michigan in 1991, an eighth-grader whose growth spurt had taken him from stocky to slim but was still too insecure to even bother trying out for the basketball team.So you can imagine how blown away I was when those five iconic teenagers -- Chris Webber, Jalen Rose, Juwon Howard, Jimmy King and Ray Jackson -- hit the court for the Wolverines and became a cultural phenomenon.I know I wasn’t alone.I never did become a basketball stud, let alone a U-M fan, but the Fab Five still elicits the kind of youthful nostalgia that must be felt by a whole generation, especially in the state of Michigan.For two years, the Fab Five not only were must-see TV, they were must-emulate. Black socks? Check. Baggy shorts? Mercifully, check. Swagger and bravado, even if it was painfully phony and empty? Check.The Fab Five had its share of critics -- boy, did they ever -- but odds are there were an equal number of fans.Both sides will be able to relive that infamous period when ESPN premieres "The Fab Five" at 9 p.m. Sunday. The two-hour film examines the rise and fall of the group that revolutionized college basketball, from the recruitment process that brought them to Ann Arbor, to the notorious Webber timeout and the scandal that tarnished everything."This is almost like the Bible of the Fab Five story," Rose said during a national conference call this week. "We really went in-depth about everything -- the good, the bad, the ugly."The documentary certainly doesn’t pull any punches. It opens with King candidly talking about the university taking down the pair of Final Four banners in the wake of the Ed Martin scandal: "It’s like they snatched your life dreams away. When you mess up, there are consequences and know that you can pay for them by being erased."Strong words, but the memories of the Fab Five will not be wiped from anyone’s memory any time soon.ESPN’s special ensures that by packing in loads of highlights, rarely-seen clips of the Fab Five in high school and frank interviews with former U-M coaches Steve Fisher, Brian Dutcher and Perry Watson and rap icons Ice Cube and Chuck D.There is a void, however, since Webber chose not to take part, and his absence creates an obvious hole throughout the show."He felt like at this time, he didn’t want to speak and talk about his portrayal or how things went those couple of seasons," said Rose, who also serves as a producer. "But to protect the integrity of the story, the story still went on. The story is about '91-93, not about 2011."The special also suffers from a lack of outside perspective. After all, who wouldn’t want to hear recollections and insights from the likes of Bobby Knight, Dick Vitale and Jimmy Jackson? Or Christian Laettner, who the Fab Five call soft, pretty boy and a few other descriptions that wouldn’t be described as family friendly.But, as Rose points out, they had a hard enough time fitting everything into the two-hour window. (What, like people wouldn’t have watched a five-hour special? Maybe they’re saving it for the DVD.)Regardless, "The Fab Five" is worth catching, if only to see how much Rose, Howard, King and Jackson have grown. They speak thoughtfully and articulately about the racism they endured, the disappointments they experienced in back-to-back national title games, and the exploitation they felt as the university pulled in millions in merchandise sales while they got nothing.Two decades ago, the Fab Five changed the way people looked at college basketball.ESPN’s documentary should change the way people look at the Fab Five.HBO tackles college basketballNot to be outdone, HBO will debut its own documentary, "Runnin’ Rebels of UNLV" at 9:30 p.m. Saturday. The hour-long special revisits Las Vegas from 1973-92, when UNLV utilized its own brash, swaggering attitude to climb to the top of the college basketbal ladder.Sound familiar? While ESPN’s "The Fab Five" focuses mainly on the players, "Runnin’ Rebels of UNLV" largely revolves around legendary coach Jerry Tarkanian.But the similarities between UNLV and Michigan are almost eerie, from the rock star personalities to the Us. vs. Them mentality to the showdowns with Duke.It’s another outstanding sports documentary from HBO. By now, we wouldn’t expect anything less.E-mail Michael Zuidema: mzuidema@grpress.com and follow him on Twitter at twitter.com/michaelzuidema
